episode_title: Four Papers That Changed the World

stories.title: Friedman's 1968 Speech
stories.description: Ajay narrates the story of Milton Friedman's presidential address to the American Economic Association in 1968. At a time when Keynesianism was dominant and failing, Friedman introduced a new paradigm: people are not dumb, they optimize, and policy must account for their reactions.

stories.title: Hayek and Wittgenstein in the Trenches
stories.description: Amit shares an anecdote about F.A. Hayek and Ludwig Wittgenstein serving together in World War I. He mentions Wittgenstein's diaries from the trenches, which, contrary to high philosophy, were filled with mundane human desires.

stories.title: The Candlemakers' Petition
stories.description: Amit recounts Frederic Bastiat's famous satirical petition where candlemakers ask the government to block out the sun to protect their industry from 'unfair competition', illustrating the absurdity of protectionism.

stories.title: The Broken Window
stories.description: The classic parable by Bastiat: A boy breaks a window. People say it's good for the economy because the glazier gets paid. Bastiat points out the 'unseen': what the shopkeeper would have bought (e.g., shoes) if he hadn't had to replace the window.

stories.title: Candy Crush and Opportunity Cost
stories.description: Amit uses a personal example to explain opportunity cost: playing Candy Crush gives immediate pleasure (the seen) but makes his future self 'stupider' by taking time away from reading or writing (the unseen).

recommendations.comment: F.A. Hayek's classic warning that central planning leads to authoritarianism.
Ludwig von Mises's book that converted Hayek from a socialist to a classical liberal.
Matt Ridley's book on how bottom-up evolution explains everything from language to the economy.
Henry Hazlitt's accessible introduction to economics, heavily inspired by Bastiat.

recommendations.item: GOAT: Who is the Greatest Economist of all Time?
recommendations.comment: Tyler Cowen's book profiling major economists. Recommended by Ajay as a great starting point.
Online platform by Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok for learning economics. Highly recommended by Amit.

core_ideas.description: Monetary policy should not try to manage the business cycle or unemployment (real variables) but should focus on a single mandate: controlling inflation (nominal variable) to provide stability.
Knowledge in society is dispersed among millions of individuals (time and place). No central planner can aggregate this information to make efficient decisions.
Prices are a communication mechanism that coordinates economic activity without central direction. They are 'signals wrapped in incentives'.

Firms exist because using the market (bargaining, contracting) is costly. Inside a firm, these transaction costs are replaced by authority/hierarchy. The boundary of the firm is determined by where these costs balance out.
Good economics requires looking beyond the immediate, visible effects of a policy (the seen) to the long-term, indirect consequences (the unseen/opportunity cost).
Complex, orderly systems (like language or the market) emerge from the bottom up through the interaction of individuals, without being designed by anyone.

jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Amit joking that when people hear 'Hayek', they shouldn't think of the actress Salma Hayek.
Similar joke distinguishing the actress from the socialist economist.
Reference to Leonard Read's famous essay about how no single person knows how to make a pencil.
Amit's observation that the great philosopher's war diaries were mostly about base desires.
